plants.title: Mulberry
idCues: Fruit looks like a slim blackberry; ripens white → red → deep purple-black.
Look down for purple stains on the sidewalk — they give the tree away before you spot the fruit.
Leaves are serrated and often mitten-lobed — unlobed, single-lobed and double-lobed leaves can all appear on the same tree.
Milky sap in the leaf stem when snapped.
safety: Very safe fruit. Unripe (white/green) berries and the milky sap can cause mild stomach upset — eat only fully soft, dark fruit.
plants.body:
The single best "hidden fruit" of the July city. Mulberries are planted as street and yard trees all over, and most people never notice them until the sidewalk underneath turns purple.

## Harvest
- Ripe fruit is **soft and drops at a touch**. Lay a sheet or open umbrella under a branch and shake — ripe berries rain down, unripe ones stay put.
- **Branches out of reach on a tall tree?** Spread the sheet as wide as you can, then hook a high limb with a long pole, rake, or walking cane and jostle it — or shake the trunk of a smaller tree. Only dead-ripe berries let go, so you're auto-sorting for ripeness; come back in a few days for the rest.
- Fruit ripens unevenly over 2–3 weeks, so the same tree keeps giving. Beat the birds in the morning.
- They **stain everything** — fingers, clothes, car roofs. Wear old clothes; park elsewhere.

## Prep
- Eat fresh by the handful. They're delicate and don't keep — refrigerate and use within a day or two.
- Freeze on a tray then bag for smoothies / baking.
- Slightly low in acidity, so cook with a squeeze of lemon for jam or to brighten a pie. Great in muffins, over yogurt, or as a quick compote.

## Notes
_(Log the trees you find here — location, how loaded, when it ripened.)_

plants.title: Lamb's Quarters
idCues: Diamond / goosefoot-shaped leaves, often with a slightly toothed edge.
The diagnostic: a white, powdery, water-repellent coating on the newest growth and leaf undersides — rub the growing tip and it feels mealy, and water beads on it.
Stems often striped with pink/magenta; can grow knee- to head-high in disturbed soil.
safety: One of the safest wild greens — a close relative of quinoa and spinach. Like spinach it contains oxalates, so cook it and don't eat huge amounts raw daily.
No dangerous lookalike, but confirm the mealy coating; avoid plants from sprayed or roadside soil (it accumulates nitrates).
plants.body:
Arguably the best wild green on the continent, growing as a "weed" in every garden bed, vacant lot, and sidewalk edge — abundant right now. If you learn one urban green, learn this one.

## Harvest
- Pick the tender top 10–15 cm and young leaves; strip leaves from tougher lower stems.
- It regrows after cutting, so a good patch keeps producing all season.
- Later in the season it sets abundant seeds — edible, a wild relative of quinoa, worth collecting if you're keen.

## Prep
- Cook exactly like spinach: sauté with garlic and oil, wilt into soups, eggs, dal, or pasta. It holds texture better than spinach.
- Young leaves are fine raw in small amounts, but cooking is the default (reduces oxalates, tastes better).

## Notes
_(Best patches, and when they bolt to seed.)_

plants.title: Purslane
idCues: Low, spreading mat in sidewalk cracks, gravel, and garden beds.
Smooth, fat, succulent paddle-shaped leaves and thick reddish stems — the whole plant is juicy.
Snap a stem: no milky sap (that helps rule out the toxic lookalike below).
safety: Lookalike — spurge (Euphorbia): also mats in sidewalks but has thin, non-succulent leaves and bleeds milky white sap when broken, which purslane never does. If it oozes white, it's not purslane.
Purslane is high in oxalates like spinach — fine in normal amounts, moderate if you're prone to kidney stones.
plants.body:
A crunchy, lemony succulent growing free in the cracks of the city, and one of the richest plant sources of omega-3 fatty acids. Most people weed it out without knowing it's a delicacy (it's sold in markets in Mexico and the Mediterranean).

## Harvest
- Pinch off the tender stem tips and leaves; it regrows readily from what's left.
- Harvest from clean ground — since it grows at foot level in sidewalks, avoid dog-traffic spots and rinse very well.

## Prep
- **Raw:** whole sprigs in salads — crisp, juicy, lemon-tart. Great with tomato, cucumber, feta.
- **Cooked:** thickens soups and stews slightly (a mild okra-like effect); good sautéed, in stir-fries, or folded into eggs.
- Classic Mexican *verdolagas* — stewed with tomatillo and pork.

## Notes
_(Cleanest patches you trust.)_

plants.title: Apple
plants.season: Fruit ripe late summer into fall (windfalls can start dropping late July)

gallery.caption: Young apple tree in the row along the bike path.

idCues: Full-size apples (3–8 cm), green ripening to yellow/red; hang singly or in small clusters.
Toothed oval leaves, greyish bark; white-pink 5-petal apple blossom in spring.
Feral/planted apples along paths and parkland are often an unnamed seedling — flavour ranges from sweet to sharp; taste before you commit to a bagful.
safety: Flesh is edible. Like all apples, the seeds contain trace cyanogenic compounds — don't eat handfuls of crushed seeds; the fruit itself is fine.
Check windfalls for bruising and worm holes before eating raw — bruised drops are best cooked.
plants.body:
A row of young apple trees lines the bike path (on the map) — planted or feral, either way left unpicked. Full-size apples, not crabapples, so a handful is a real snack. Fruit is on and windfalls are already dropping to the grass below.

## Harvest
- Pick when fully coloured and they part from the branch with an easy twist. Taste one first — seedling apples run anywhere from sweet to sharp-tart.
- Grab the good ones off the tree; use windfalls quickly (they bruise) and cook rather than eat those raw.
- They hold and sweeten on the tree into fall — apples that get a frost turn noticeably sweeter.

## Prep
- **Raw** if the tree's a sweet one — otherwise they shine cooked: sauce, apple butter, pie, or a tart-sweet crumble.
- Slightly under-ripe or sharp apples are high in pectin and perfect stretched into **jelly** or added to a low-pectin fruit to help it set.
- Halve and core; no need to peel for sauce (run it through a mill after cooking).

## Notes
_(Note which of the row's trees are sweet-enough-raw vs. cook-only, and when they peak.)_

plants.title: Chicory
plants.season: Greens spring & fall; flowers summer; roots dug in fall
idCues: Sky-blue, strap-shaped ray florets with 5 tiny square-toothed tips — that pale periwinkle blue is nearly unique among roadside plants. Flowers open in the morning and often close by afternoon.
Flower heads sit sessile (stalkless), clasped tight against the stem along a stiff, wiry, nearly leafless flowering stalk.
Rigid, angular, sparsely bristly stems; a basal rosette of dandelion-like lobed leaves, with small clasping leaves up the stem. Broken stems and roots ooze bitter white latex.
Loves dry, sunny, disturbed ground — roadsides, rail edges, vacant lots.
safety: No dangerous lookalikes — the blue flowers plus milky latex are unmistakable. It's the same species as cultivated Belgian endive / radicchio.
Every part is bitter; older leaves are intensely so. Skip plants growing in sprayed verges or exhaust-heavy roadsides.
plants.body:
A cheerful roadside weed that's fully edible root-to-flower — and the classic wild coffee substitute. Blooming its sky-blue flowers right now across sunny urban edges.

## Harvest
- **Leaves:** best from the basal rosette in early spring and again in cool fall — young leaves are pleasantly bitter, older summer leaves punishingly so.
- **Roots:** dig in fall from established plants; a thick taproot, like a pale carrot.
- **Flowers:** pick fresh in the morning for a garnish.

## Prep
- **Greens:** treat like dandelion or radicchio — braise, sauté, or blanch-and-refresh to tame the bitterness; toss young leaves into salad in small amounts.
- **Roasted-root "coffee":** scrub, chop, roast the root until dark and brittle, grind, and brew like coffee — caffeine-free, deep and roasty. The traditional New Orleans coffee cut.
- **Flowers:** scatter over salads as a garnish.

## Notes
_(Best rosette patches for spring greens; which plants have the fattest roots for fall digging.)_

plants.title: Crabapple

gallery.caption: Loaded crabapple at rue de Verdun & Beatty.

idCues: Small apples, from pea- to golf-ball size, red / yellow / green; hang in clusters.
Classic apple-blossom in spring (white-pink, 5 petals); toothed oval leaves.
A 'crabapple' is just any apple under ~5 cm — all are edible, they range sour to sweet-tart.
safety: Flesh is edible. Like all apples, the seeds contain trace cyanogenic compounds — don't eat handfuls of crushed seeds; the fruit itself is fine.
plants.body:
Ornamental crabapples line streets and parks all over Verdun — two are already on the map (Gaétan-Laberge and rue de Verdun & Beatty). Most are ignored and left to drop, which makes them a reliable, high-yield forage.

## Harvest
- Pick when fully coloured and slightly soft; a good tree gives kilos. Taste one first — some cultivars are mouth-puckeringly tart (great cooked), others pleasant raw.
- They hold on the tree well into fall, sweetening after the first frost.

## Prep
- **Crabapple jelly** is the classic — they're loaded with natural pectin, so jelly sets with no added pectin. Simmer whole, strain, add sugar, set.
- Also great: apple butter, sauce, chutney, or muddled into cider/shrubs. Halve and core the bigger ones; tiny ones just simmer whole and strain.

## Notes
_(Note which trees are sweet-enough-raw vs. cook-only, and ripening dates.)_

plants.title: Linden / Basswood
plants.season: Flowers early summer; young leaves spring
idCues: Very common street tree with a distinctive asymmetric heart-shaped leaf (lopsided base).
Flowers hang from a papery, tongue-shaped bract (wing) — unmistakable once seen.
Fragrant creamy flowers in early summer; heavily buzzing with bees when in bloom.
safety: Flowers and young leaves are safe and mild. Old / heavily-scented flowers can taste bitter; harvest fresh, just-open blooms.
plants.body:
The friendliest street tree to forage — nothing about it is dangerous, and it gives two things: a lovely calming tea from the flowers, and a mild salad green from the spring leaves.

## Harvest
- **Flowers:** pick with their papery bract in early summer, on a dry day, just as they open. Dry in a single layer out of sun for tea.
- **Leaves:** the tender, translucent young spring leaves are the salad ones; older leaves get tough.

## Prep
- **Linden flower tea (tilleul):** steep a small handful of dried flowers in just-off-boil water 5 min. Mild, honeyed, faintly floral — a traditional evening/calming tea.
- Young leaves go straight into salads or sandwiches — soft and mild, a good bulk green.

## Notes
_(Mark bloom timing — the flower window is short.)_

plants.title: Wood Sorrel
idCues: Looks like clover but leaflets are heart-shaped (clover's are oval/rounded with a pale crescent).
Three leaflets that fold down along their midrib in evening / bright sun.
Small 5-petalled yellow flowers; tiny okra-like upright seed pods.
Tastes bright and lemony — the giveaway.
safety: Safe as a trailside nibble. Contains oxalic acid (the tang), so it's a garnish/snack, not a bulk green — don't eat bowlfuls.
plants.body:
The little lemony clover-lookalike growing in lawns, cracks, and garden edges. A fun, safe, instantly-rewarding nibble — the bright sour hit makes it a favourite for kids and a nice trail snack.

## Harvest
- Pinch leaves, flowers, and young seed pods — all edible and all tangy.
- Grows everywhere; take a little as you pass.

## Prep
- Eat raw as a trail nibble, scatter over salads, or use as a lemony garnish on fish and soups.
- Steep a handful in cold water for a lightly sour "lemonade."

## Notes
_(Nothing to log really — it's everywhere. A good confidence plant.)_

plants.title: Broadleaf Plantain
idCues: Ground-hugging rosette of broad oval leaves with strong parallel veins that run leaf-tip to stem.
Pull a leaf apart slowly — the veins stay as stringy threads.
A narrow 'rat-tail' flower/seed spike stands up from the centre.
safety: Extremely safe — the classic beginner 'confidence plant', nearly impossible to confuse. (Not related to the banana-plantain.)
plants.body:
The most reliable "I know exactly what this is" plant in any lawn or path edge. Best known as a first-aid herb, but the young leaves are also edible.

## Harvest
- Pick young, tender inner leaves (older ones get stringy and tough).
- The green seed spikes can be stripped and eaten too, or dried — the seeds are a psyllium relative (fibre).

## Uses
- **Drawing poultice:** chew or crush a leaf and press onto insect bites, stings, and minor scrapes — a classic field remedy for the itch/sting. Genuinely useful on a foraging walk.
- **Food:** young leaves cooked like a green (blanch to soften), or shredded small into salad.

## Notes
_(Confidence plant — no need to log spots.)_

plants.title: Red Raspberry
plants.season: Ripe July–Aug (often a lighter second flush into fall)

gallery.caption: Ripe red berry ready to pull off hollow.
Cane and toothed leaflets — white-woolly beneath.

idCues: Arching, thorny canes (usually round, with fine bristly prickles); grows in thickets.
Leaves compound with 3–5 toothed leaflets, distinctly white-woolly underneath — the key tell.
Ripe berry is red and pulls off the core hollow, like a little thimble (blackberry keeps its core; that's the difference).
safety: No toxic raspberry lookalikes — the whole bramble (Rubus) group is edible. Nothing dangerous mimics it here.
Even the leaves are safe (traditional raspberry-leaf tea). The only caution is wilted Rubus leaves, which can be mildly upsetting — use fresh or fully dried, not in-between.
plants.body:
The easiest, safest wild berry there is — if it looks like a raspberry, it is one. Grazing on the spot is the whole point; anything past that is a bonus.

## Harvest
- Pick when **fully red and it detaches with the lightest tug**, leaving a hollow thimble. If you have to pull, it's not ready.
- Morning is best (firmer, cooler). Bring a shallow container — they crush easily.
- Watch the thorns and check for the odd insect inside; a quick float-rinse sorts them out.

## Prep
- Best eaten straight off the cane. Beyond that: over yogurt/oatmeal, into pancakes, or a quick fridge jam.
- Freeze on a tray then bag, so they don't clump — great through winter.

## Notes
- Canes are biennial: this year's fruiting canes die back, new ones take over — so a good patch produces year after year.
- _(Verdun brambles logged Aug 4 — ripe now.)_

plants.title: Aronia / Black Chokeberry
plants.season: Ripe Aug–Sep; fruit hangs on into fall

gallery.caption: Purple-black pomes with the star-scar tip; glossy toothed leaves.
Loose flat clusters ripening along the branch.

idCues: Medium multi-stem shrub, usually waist-to-head height.
Glossy, finely-toothed elliptical leaves; look for tiny dark glands along the midrib on the upper surface (a chokeberry hallmark).
Berries are pea-sized, matte-to-glossy purple-black, in loose flat clusters — each with a small 5-pointed star scar at the tip (it's a tiny pome, like a mini apple).
Fall foliage turns brilliant red — the shrub lights up.
safety: Edible and safe — the name 'chokeberry' is about taste, not toxicity: raw fruit is intensely astringent and mouth-drying, not poisonous.

Don't confuse with buckthorn (Rhamnus/Frangula), a common invasive with similar dark berries — buckthorn berries are laxative. Chokeberry's star-tipped pome + glossy toothed leaf + red-glandular midrib separate it; buckthorn berries have several hard seeds and no star scar.
plants.body:
Aronia is one of the great under-appreciated urban berries — commonly planted as a landscape shrub, so it's everywhere, and almost nobody picks it. Raw it's ferociously astringent (that's the "choke"), but it's one of the highest-antioxidant fruits going, and it transforms completely once cooked or sweetened.

## Harvest
- Pick when berries are fully **purple-black and slightly soft**, August into September. They hold on the bush for weeks, so there's no rush.
- Whole clusters strip off easily. A frost sweetens them and knocks back the astringency — like rowan, it's worth waiting or freezing the pick overnight.

## Prep
- **Raw:** edible but drying — a nibble is fine, a handful is a pucker. Best mixed into other things.
- **Juice / syrup:** the classic use — deep ruby, tart, great cut with apple or added to sparkling water.
- **Jam & baking:** cook down with sugar (and pectin-rich apple/crabapple) into a dark preserve; or fold into muffins, oatmeal, smoothies.
- **Dried:** dehydrate for a chewy raisin-like snack that mellows the astringency.

## Notes
- Very high in anthocyanins/vitamin C — the health-food "aronia" powders are this exact berry.
- _(Two patches logged on the Aug 4 Verdun walk — see the map.)_

plants.title: Blackberry
idCues: Thorny, arching biennial canes forming dense thickets on edges and clearings
Aggregate berry of many small drupelets; ripens green to red to glossy black
Picked fruit stays SOLID — it keeps its white core (torus), unlike a raspberry which pulls off hollow
Compound leaves with 3–5 toothed leaflets; white five-petalled flowers in spring
safety: No toxic lookalikes; the main hazard is the thorns — wear long sleeves
Eat only fully black, soft berries — red or shiny-firm ones are sour and unripe
Wash fruit from roadsides or sprayed areas; avoid canes overhanging dog-walked paths
plants.body:
## Harvest
Work the sunny edges of thickets, trails, and railway margins from early August on. Ripe blackberries are dull-black, plump, and detach with the gentlest tug; if you have to pull, leave it another day. The give-away versus a black raspberry: a picked blackberry stays **solid** — it keeps its pale central core — while a raspberry slips off hollow like a thimble. Bring a container you don't mind staining and expect thorns.

## Prep
Eat them warm off the cane. At home, rinse gently and use within a day or two — they mould fast. They freeze well spread on a tray, and cook down into jam, cobbler, or a sauce for yogurt. Seeds are noticeable; strain if you want a smooth coulis.

## Notes
Canes are biennial: first-year shoots leaf out, second-year canes fruit then die. Come back to a good patch yearly. Compare with the red raspberry guide — same genus, opposite core.

plants.title: Serviceberry / Saskatoon

gallery.caption: Mapped bush near the Verdun riverfront — red pomes with the star-crown tip.

idCues: Small tree / multi-stem shrub, hugely common as an ornamental planting.
Berries look like blueberries but with a 5-pointed star crown at the tip (like an apple's calyx); ripen red → purple.
Spring tell: white flowers with five narrow, strappy petals, appearing before leaves fully open.
Leaves oval, finely toothed, soft; smooth grey bark often with faint vertical striping.
safety: Edible and delicious. Seeds have a faint almond note (trace cyanogenic compounds) — normal to eat, just don't binge on crushed seeds.
plants.body:
One of the best native berries and planted everywhere as an ornamental — but it ripens **late June to early July**, so by late July you've likely missed this year's window. The move now: **note the bushes** and come back next June.

There's already one on the map near the Verdun riverfront.

## Harvest
- Ripe berries are deep purple and soft, and come off with a gentle roll of the fingers.
- Birds love them — a well-placed bush can be stripped in a day when ripe, so check daily as they turn.

## Prep
- Eat fresh; flavour is like a sweeter, almondy blueberry.
- Classic in pies, muffins, pancakes, and jam (the prairie "saskatoon pie"). Freeze exactly like blueberries.

## Notes
_(Mark bloom date and ripening date each year — that's how you catch the window.)_

plants.title: Red Currant
idCues: Translucent, jewel-red berries hanging in strings (racemes) of 8–15
Lobed, maple-like leaves with 3–5 pointed lobes; thornless stems
Small green-yellow flowers in spring, also in drooping clusters
Common garden escape along fences, hedges, and yard edges
safety: No dangerous lookalikes; thornless and easy to identify by the hanging red strings
Tart and safe raw, though sour enough that most people prefer it cooked
Only harvest from clearly unsprayed hedges and fence lines
plants.body:
## Harvest
Look along fences, alley edges, and old garden borders where a cultivated bush has gone feral. The fruit is unmistakable: clear red berries strung on delicate stems like tiny grapes, over maple-shaped leaves on thornless wood. Pick whole strings by the stem rather than individual berries — it's faster and gentler on the fruit. They hold on the bush well, so you have a wide window.

## Prep
Red currants are sharply tart raw — good in small amounts, but they shine cooked. They're loaded with natural pectin, so they jelly beautifully with just sugar and no added setting agent. Simmer, strain out the seeds and skins, and you get a bright, clean jelly. They also lift into sauces, cordials, and baking.

## Notes
Strip the berries off the stem with a fork before cooking. A single established bush can yield generously year after year.

plants.title: Black Currant

gallery.caption: Glossy black berries in a short cluster on aromatic maple-lobed leaves.

idCues: Thornless shrub (currants have no prickles — that separates them from gooseberries).
Leaves palmate and maple-like, with 3–5 pointed toothed lobes; crush one — black currant leaves are strongly, resinously aromatic (the classic cassis smell).
Berries smooth, round, glossy black, in short hanging clusters (small racemes), each keeping a little dried flower-tail at the tip.
safety: Edible and safe — currants (Ribes) have no toxic lookalikes in this group; the fruit is a well-known cultivated berry.

Confirm the aromatic leaf + thornless stem + black berries in short strings. This is likely a garden-escape R. nigrum; the native American black currant (R. americanum) is equally edible, so exact species doesn't affect eating.
plants.body:
Cassis — the intensely aromatic black berry behind the liqueur and the jam. Escaped garden plants turn up in hedges and along fences; the crush-and-smell test makes it one of the easier berries to confirm.

## Harvest
- Pick when berries are fully **black, glossy and soft**, mid-to-late summer. Ripe ones come off easily; strip whole strings and sort later.
- The flavour is much more assertive than a store raspberry — sharp, musky, "grown-up." A little goes a long way.

## Prep
- **Raw:** edible but tart and resinous — most people prefer them cooked or sweetened.
- **Jam / cassis syrup:** the classic. High in pectin, so they set well.
- **Cordial / infusions:** steep in sugar syrup (or spirit, for a homemade crème de cassis).
- **Leaves:** a few aromatic young leaves make a fragrant tea.

## Notes
- Very high in vitamin C.
- _(Verdun hedge logged Aug 4, next to the raspberry brambles.)_

plants.title: Wild Strawberry
idCues: Tiny red berries, a fraction the size of cultivated ones but intensely sweet and aromatic
WHITE five-petalled flowers
Toothed trifoliate leaves (three leaflets); spreads by runners over the ground
Seeds sit in small pits on the berry's surface, not raised above it
safety: No dangerous lookalikes
Mock strawberry (Potentilla indica / Duchesnea) is a harmless but disappointing double: it has YELLOW flowers and bland, watery, seedy fruit whose seeds stick OUT
True wild strawberry has WHITE flowers and unmistakable strawberry aroma and flavour — use scent and taste to confirm
plants.body:
## Harvest
Hunt sunny lawns, meadow edges, and trail verges in June. The plants hug the ground and spread by runners, so a single find usually means a whole colony. The berries are small — pea to fingernail sized — and easy to miss under the leaves, but each one packs more flavour than a supermarket strawberry. Pick only deep-red, soft, fragrant fruit; pale ones are sour.

## Prep
Honestly, most get eaten on the spot. If you gather enough, they're extraordinary over yogurt, folded into pancakes, or macerated with a little sugar. They don't keep — use them the same day.

## Notes
Before picking, check the flower and the smell. WHITE flowers plus real strawberry aroma = the genuine article. YELLOW flowers with bland, seedy, stick-out fruit = mock strawberry — safe to eat but a letdown, not worth the basket space.

plants.title: Plum

gallery.caption: Purple plum with waxy bloom on a street tree, early August.

idCues: Round fruit 2–5 cm with a dusty, powdery bloom you can rub off, a single flattened stone, and one shallow seam running down the side. Colour ranges purple, blue-black, red, or yellow.
Oval, finely-toothed leaves; new growth and twigs often reddish. Bark dark with horizontal lenticels.
Spring: clusters of white 5-petal blossoms, before or with the leaves.
Tells it apart from cherry / chokecherry: plums are larger, hang mostly singly, and have a flattened seamed stone — cherries dangle in clusters on long stalks with round pits.
safety: Flesh is edible raw and cooked. Like all Prunus, the stone/seed, leaves, and twigs contain cyanogenic compounds — don't crush and eat the pits.
Wild and ornamental plums range from sweet to mouth-puckering; astringency fades when the fruit is dead-ripe (soft, easily pulled) and disappears with cooking. Try one before picking a bagful.
plants.body:
Cultivated and feral plums turn up as street and yard trees all over Montréal — an escaped orchard plum or an ornamental cherry-plum will fruit heavily and mostly go unpicked. One's on the map now (a loaded purple-plum street tree), with green immature fruit still ripening alongside the first ripe ones in early August.

## Harvest
- Pick when the fruit is fully coloured, gives to a gentle squeeze, and pulls off easily. Under-ripe plums are hard and astringent — leave them a week.
- Ripening runs roughly August into September depending on the tree; a single tree drops over a couple of weeks, so check back.
- Watch for wasps on windfalls and split skins after rain.

## Prep
- Best fresh off the tree when dead-ripe. Otherwise: jam, compote, plum butter, or roasted with the stones out.
- Tart/astringent cultivars are cook-only — they make excellent jam and sauce, and a good hedgerow gin/vodka.
- Halve and twist to pop the stone; a clingstone type may need cutting around.

## Notes
_(Note which trees are sweet-enough-raw vs. cook-only, and their ripening dates.)_

plants.title: Rowan / Mountain-Ash
plants.season: Berries colour up Aug–Sep; best after first frost, hold on the tree into winter

gallery.caption: Flat-topped clusters of orange pomes with the star-crown tip; finely toothed pinnate leaflets.
Whole tree beside the path, berries colouring up.

idCues: Small-to-medium tree; smooth greyish bark, often multi-stemmed.
Pinnate compound leaves — a central stalk lined with ~11–17 paired, finely serrated leaflets.
Dense, flat-topped clusters of small (~8 mm) orange-red berries (pomes), each with a tiny 5-pointed star at the tip.
Very common as a park and street tree across Montréal.
safety: Not for raw eating in quantity — intensely bitter/astringent, and raw berries contain parasorbic acid (irritating, can upset the stomach).
Cooking neutralises the parasorbic acid into harmless sorbic acid; a frost (or a stint in the freezer) also mellows the bitterness. Cooked = safe and traditional.
ID together: pinnate leaves + flat orange pome clusters. Don't confuse with unrelated ornamentals you can't vouch for.
plants.body:
Rowan is a classic hedgerow and street tree — the orange berry clusters are unmistakable in late summer. Edible, but firmly in the **cook-don't-graze** camp: raw they're harshly bitter and a little irritating, but cooked (ideally after a frost) they make one of the great wild preserves.

## Harvest
- Cut whole clusters once the berries are fully orange-red and slightly soft, **August into fall**. They hold on the tree for months, so there's no rush.
- Best flavour comes **after the first frost** — or cheat it by freezing the picked berries overnight, which breaks down the bitterness the same way.
- Strip the berries off the stalks before cooking (the stalks are bitter).

## Prep
- **Rowan jelly** is the classic: a tart, faintly bitter amber preserve, traditionally served with game, lamb, and rich cheeses. Rowan is high in pectin, so it sets well — or blend with crabapple for extra set and a softer flavour.
- Also good cooked into a sharp sauce or added to apple dishes for a bittersweet edge.
- High in vitamin C.

## Notes
- Never eat more than a nibble raw — bitter and stomach-upsetting.
- _(Log the first-frost date each year — that's your cue that the berries have sweetened.)_

plants.title: Chokecherry
plants.season: Fruit ripens late July–Sep, colouring dark red to near-black

gallery.caption: Ripe dark clusters — many cherries on a single drooping raceme; finely toothed oval leaves.
Growing along the community-garden fence, fruit colouring up.

idCues: Large shrub or small tree, often thicket-forming; smooth greyish bark.
Simple, oval, finely serrated leaves with a pointed tip — alternate, glossy dark green above.
Fruit hangs in elongated cylindrical clusters (racemes) — many small cherries on one drooping stalk, ripening red → dark purple-black.
Each cherry has a single hard stone. Ripe fruit is sweet-then-astringent — puckers the mouth (the 'choke').
safety: Never eat the pits / stones. The seeds, leaves, and twigs contain cyanogenic compounds (amygdalin) that release cyanide — toxic if crushed and swallowed in quantity.

The flesh is fine, but the fruit is astringent raw — chokecherry is a cook-and-strain plant. Cooking whole fruit for jelly/syrup is traditional and safe (you strain out the stones); never purée or crack the pits.
Wilted leaves are the real hazard to livestock — not something foragers eat, but worth knowing the whole plant is cyanogenic apart from the ripe flesh.
plants.body:
Chokecherry is one of the most common wild cherries across Montréal — thickets of it line paths, fences, and riverbanks. The giveaway is the fruit habit: instead of single cherries, the small dark fruits hang in long **grape-like racemes**. Named for the astringent "choke" when you bite a raw one — but cooked and strained, it makes a gorgeous deep-red jelly and syrup.

## Harvest
- Pick whole clusters once the cherries are **dark purple to nearly black** and slightly soft — late July through September here.
- Strip the fruit off the stalks. It's fiddly but fast once a cluster is fully ripe.
- Taste one for ripeness (spit the pit): ripe flesh is sweet up front, then puckery. Under-ripe red fruit is harshly astringent — leave it.

## Prep
- **Chokecherry jelly / syrup** is the classic: simmer the whole fruit with a little water, then strain through a jelly bag so the stones and skins are left behind. Cook the strained juice with sugar (and pectin — chokecherry is only moderately high) for jelly, or reduce for syrup.
- Also good in wild-fruit blends, sauces for game, or fruit leather (strained purée only — **never** pass the pits through).
- Deep colour and a distinctive almond-tinged cherry flavour.

## Safety
- **Do not crush or eat the pits.** Like other stone fruit in the *Prunus* family, the seeds are cyanogenic. Whole-fruit cooking and straining removes them — that's the whole point of the method.
- Everything green (leaves, twigs) is also cyanogenic; only the ripe flesh is food.

## Notes
- Distinguish from black cherry (*Prunus serotina*), which is a tall tree with similar racemes — both are prepared the same way, so an ID mix-up here is low-stakes as long as you cook and strain.

plants.title: Rose Hips
plants.season: Hips colour up Sep; best after the first frosts, hold into winter

gallery.caption: Green hips still swelling — the sepal crown at the tip is the tell.
Prickly stems and pinnate, toothed rose leaflets.

idCues: Thorny arching shrub; leaves pinnate with 5–7 (sometimes 9) toothed leaflets on a stalk — like a small rowan leaf but prickly.
The 'hip' is the swollen fruit left behind after the flower drops: an oval-to-round pod that ripens from green → orange → deep red.
Look for the dried sepal 'crown' at the tip of each hip and the remains of the rose flower.
safety: All true rose (Rosa) hips are edible — no toxic rose lookalikes. It's one of the safest wild fruits to ID (unmistakable thorny pinnate-leaved shrub with a red flower-pod).

Remove the seeds/inner hairs before eating the flesh: the fine hairs around the seeds are a known irritant (the original 'itching powder'). Either scrape the flesh off the seeds, or cook whole and strain.
plants.body:
**What a rose hip is:** the fruit of a rose. Once the flower's petals fall, the base swells into a little red pod — that's the hip. It's a "berry" only loosely; botanically it's a fleshy pod packed with seeds. The thin outer flesh is the edible part, and it's one of the richest wild sources of **vitamin C** there is (famously used for syrup during WWII when citrus was scarce).

## Harvest
- **Not yet** — the ones you photographed are still green. They colour to orange-red through September.
- Best picked **after the first frost**, when they soften and sweeten (or pick firm and freeze overnight to fake the frost). They hang on the shrub well into winter, so there's a long window.
- Bigger hips (dog rose, rugosa) are much less fiddly than tiny ones.

## Prep — mind the seeds
The catch: inside each hip is a cluster of seeds wrapped in **fine irritant hairs** you don't want to swallow. Two ways around it:
- **Whole-cook-and-strain:** simmer whole hips soft, then push through a sieve or jelly bag — the smooth pulp/juice comes through, hairs and seeds stay behind. This is the easy route for **syrup, jelly, or purée**.
- **Deseed fresh:** top-and-tail, halve, scrape out the seeds and hairs, use the shells for tea or drying.

## Uses
- **Rose-hip syrup** — the classic, spooned over yogurt/desserts or in drinks; a vitamin-C tonic.
- **Tea** — dried deseeded shells, tart and floral (often blended with hibiscus).
- **Jelly/jam** — tart, high pectin.

## Notes
- _(Verdun shrub logged Aug 4 — green now; come back after first frost.)_

plants.title: Staghorn Sumac
plants.season: Red cones ripe August, hold into winter
idCues: Big fuzzy upright cones of deep-red berries at branch tips.
Compound leaves with many toothed leaflets in a row; young twigs velvety like antler 'velvet' (hence staghorn).
Forms colonies on roadsides, embankments, and waste ground; brilliant red-orange leaves in fall.
safety: Critical: eat only red, upright, fuzzy cones. Poison sumac has white/green, drooping berries and grows in wet swampy ground — a completely different look and habitat. Red + upright + dry ground = safe.
Despite the scary name, edible sumac is unrelated to poison ivy toxicity; it's the same genus as the culinary Middle-Eastern spice.
plants.body:
The tart red spice-and-lemonade plant, ripening in **August**. Flag the colonies now (they're easy to spot) and come back when the cones deepen to firm red.

## Harvest
- Pick whole cones on a **dry day** (rain washes out the tart coating that gives the flavour). Ripe cones are deep red and firm.
- Taste-test: lick a cone — it should be distinctly sour/tart. Bland means under-ripe or rain-washed.

## Prep
- **Sumac-ade:** crush a few cones, soak in **cold** water 15–30 min (hot water pulls out bitter tannins), swish, strain through cloth, sweeten. A pink, tart, lemonade-like drink.
- **Spice:** dry the berries, rub off and grind the outer red flesh from the seeds — that red powder is the tangy *za'atar* sumac. Great on flatbread, fish, salads.

## Notes
_(Mark the colonies now; check ripeness through August.)_

plants.title: Sugar Maple
idCues: Opposite branching; classic 5-lobed leaf with smooth-edged (not toothed) sinuses
Mature bark grey, furrowed into long vertical plates
Tap in leaf-off late winter, but ID the tree the previous summer/fall while in leaf
Black maple (Acer nigrum) looks similar and taps identically
safety: Sap itself is harmless; risk is over-tapping or damaging a tree — one tap per mature trunk, drill only ~5cm deep
Don't tap boxelder near roads or trees of unknown health; know your tree before drilling
plants.body:
## Harvest
Tap in late winter, when daytime highs climb above 0°C but nights still drop below freezing — that freeze/thaw pump is what moves the sap. Drill a hole ~5cm deep at a slight upward angle, seat a spile, and hang a covered bucket. Collect the clear, faintly sweet sap daily and keep it cold. Any maple can be tapped, but sugar maple runs the highest sugar, so it's the least work to boil down. Identify the tree the prior season while it's in leaf; the trunk is anonymous in February.

## Prep
Sap is basically sweet water — boil it down hard, roughly 40:1, to reach syrup. Do the bulk boil outdoors (it throws off enormous steam) and finish gently indoors, watching the temperature so it doesn't scorch. Filter before bottling.

## Notes
Stop tapping once buds swell — sap turns off-flavoured. Black maple taps identically. A single tap won't hurt a healthy mature tree.

plants.title: Birch
idCues: Chalky white bark that peels in papery horizontal strips
Small doubly-toothed oval leaves; slender, often clumped trunks
River birch and yellow birch are also tappable
Runs later than maple — tap as the buds begin to swell
safety: Sap is safe to drink fresh; risk is over-tapping — one tap per healthy mature trunk, shallow hole, plug when done
Birch sap sours within a day or two — keep it cold and use it quickly
plants.body:
## Harvest
Tap birch after the maple run ends, as the buds swell — usually a short window in April. Drill a shallow hole, set a spile, and collect the thin, clear sap. Peeling white paper bark makes the tree easy to confirm. Don't over-tap: one tap per mature trunk, and give the tree years between visits.

## Prep
Birch sap is only about 1% sugar — roughly 100:1 to syrup, so most foragers skip syruping and instead drink it fresh, or lightly ferment it into a country wine or a mildly fizzy tonic. If you do reduce it, go low and slow; its sugars scorch far more easily than maple's, so finish gently.

## Notes
Use it fast — birch sap sours within a day or two even refrigerated. River birch and yellow birch tap the same way. Plug the hole with a whittled peg when the run ends.

plants.title: Hackberry
idCues: Corky, warty ridged bark — the most reliable field mark
Small pea-size drupes on long individual stalks, ripening dark orange to purple
Asymmetric, toothed leaves with a long tapering tip
Fruit persists on bare branches well into winter
safety: No toxic parts, but the seed is a hard, crunchy stone — go easy on teeth and dental work
Confirm the warty bark; simply a low-risk fruit once identified
plants.body:
## Harvest
Look for small dark orange-to-purple drupes, each pea-sized on its own long stalk, from mid-September on. The tree gives itself away by its warty, corky ridged bark. Pick when the flesh has darkened; the berries persist on bare branches through winter, so this is a reliable cold-weather forage when little else is left.

## Prep
Each fruit is a thin layer of sweet, date-like flesh over a hard crunchy seed. The traditional move is to eat the whole thing — flesh and shell — and either crunch it down or grind the lot into a paste. Pounded with a little water it makes a rich "hackberry milk"; pressed into bars it's a compact trail food. The ground seed adds a nutty, almost creamy body.

## Notes
The seed is genuinely hard — grind rather than bite if you're protective of your teeth. Flavour is best after a frost or two.

plants.title: Black Cherry
idCues: Small dark cherries hanging in long drooping racemes (strings), not single-stalked
Older bark breaks into dark scaly plates likened to 'burnt cornflakes'
Finely toothed, glossy elliptical leaves; crushed twig smells of bitter almond
Single hard pit per cherry
safety: Pits, leaves, twigs, and bark are CYANOGENIC — never eat or crush the pits, and don't chew leaves or twigs
Use the flesh only; spit or strain out every pit before cooking
Wilting foliage is especially toxic to livestock — keep clippings away from animals
plants.body:
## Harvest
Black cherry ripens mid-August into September, hanging in long drooping racemes of small dark cherries — the string-of-fruit habit separates it from ornamental cherries. Confirm the tree by its older bark, which flakes into dark scaly plates often described as burnt cornflakes. Pick the darkest, softest fruit; underripe cherries are punishingly astringent.

## Prep
Raw, the flesh is thin and mouth-puckering, so black cherry is a cooking fruit. Simmer the whole cherries, then pass through a food mill or strainer to remove every pit before reducing to jelly, syrup, or a base for wine. The flavour deepens beautifully with sugar and heat.

## Notes
The pits, leaves, twigs, and bark all contain cyanogenic compounds — use the flesh only, and never crush or eat the stones. Strain thoroughly; a milled pit fragment carries the same bitter-almond toxin. Keep prunings away from grazing animals.

plants.title: Hawthorn
idCues: Small red (sometimes orange or black) pomes — 'haws' — like tiny apples
Long sharp thorns on twigs and branches
Lobed or toothed leaves; white five-petalled apple-family blossom in spring
Many species; all true haws are treated the same in the kitchen
safety: Sharp thorns — mind hands and eyes while picking
The SEEDS are cyanogenic — don't crush or eat the seeds; use the flesh only
Folk tradition uses hawthorn for the heart, but this is not medical advice — no therapeutic claims here
plants.body:
## Harvest
Haws ripen from mid-September through October — small red pomes, like miniature apples, clustered on thorny branches. There are many Crataegus species around Montréal and they're notoriously hard to tell apart, but for foraging purposes all true haws are handled alike. Watch the long thorns while you pick; gloves help.

## Prep
The flesh is mealy and mild, better cooked than eaten out of hand. Simmer the haws, then push the pulp through a sieve to leave the seeds behind, and turn it into haw jelly or a tangy haw "ketchup" for meats. The pectin-poor pulp usually wants added apple or a little pectin to set.

## Notes
The seeds are cyanogenic — sieve them out and never crush them; use flesh only. Hawthorn has a long folk reputation as a heart tonic, but treat that as lore, not medical advice.

plants.title: Wild Grape
idCues: Climbing vine with forked TENDRILS opposite the leaves
Toothed, often lobed leaves; small dark purple grapes in true bunches
Several round-to-pear-shaped seeds per grape
Common along riverbanks, fences, and woodland edges
safety: TOXIC LOOKALIKE — Canada moonseed (Menispermum canadense) vines alongside wild grape and is poisonous
Moonseed has NO tendrils, a single CRESCENT-shaped seed, non-toothed leaves, and fruit in loose sprays — grape has forked tendrils, several round/pear seeds, toothed leaves, and true bunches
Cut a berry and check the seed before eating any wild grape; when unsure, don't
plants.body:
## Harvest
Riverbank grape ripens from mid-September, hanging in true bunches of small dark purple grapes along rivers, fences, and woodland edges. Confirm the vine by its forked tendrils and toothed, often lobed leaves. Pick after the fruit softens and sweetens; earlier grapes are sharply sour but still good for jelly. Young leaves and tendrils are edible too — tendrils as a sour trail nibble, tender leaves for dolmades.

## Prep
Wild grapes are small, seedy, and tart — best as juice, jelly, or a rustic wine rather than out-of-hand eating. Simmer and strain out skins and seeds before setting the jelly. Blanched grape leaves roll around rice for stuffed dolmades.

## Notes
CRITICAL: Canada moonseed grows alongside grapes and is toxic. Moonseed has no tendrils, a single crescent-shaped seed, and non-toothed leaves, in loose sprays. Grape has forked tendrils, several round seeds, and toothed leaves in bunches. Slice a berry and check the seed every time before eating.

plants.title: Elderberry
idCues: Large multi-stem shrub; compound leaves with 5–7 (up to 11) toothed leaflets.
Now: broad, flat-topped clusters of tiny creamy-white flowers (elderflower).
Later: those flat clusters become drooping bunches of small purple-black berries by late summer.
Stems are pithy (soft white centre), not solid wood.
safety: Cook the berries — never eat raw. Raw berries, and the leaves / stems / bark, contain cyanogenic compounds that cause nausea. Cooking destroys them.
Avoid red elderberry (Sambucus racemosa — rounded, not flat, red berry clusters); treat its berries as not-for-eating.
Flat-topped white flower clusters resemble toxic carrot-family plants at a glance — but elderberry is a woody shrub with compound leaves, not a soft herb. Confirm the shrub habit.
plants.body:
A two-season plant: fragrant **elderflowers** now (fritters, cordial) and dark **elderberries** in late August–September (syrup, immune tonic). Both need a light touch — the flowers are delicate and the berries must be cooked.

## Harvest
- **Flowers:** snip whole umbels on a dry sunny morning when most florets are open and fragrant; shake out insects, don't wash (rinses off pollen/aroma). Use fresh.
- **Berries:** cut whole clusters when fully purple-black and drooping; strip berries off the stems with a fork (keep stems out — they're the bitter/toxic part).

## Prep
- **Elderflower cordial:** steep flowers with sugar, lemon, and water; strain — a classic summer syrup for spritzers.
- **Elderberry syrup:** simmer de-stemmed berries with water, strain, add honey — the well-known cold/immune syrup. Always cooked.

## Notes
_(Mark shrubs at flowering so you can return for berries.)_

plants.title: Highbush Cranberry
idCues: Shrub with maple-like, three-lobed opposite leaves
Translucent red drupes in flat-topped clusters, each holding a single flat seed
Flat-topped spring flower clusters with showy sterile outer flowers
Cooked fruit gives off a distinctive musky, sweaty smell
safety: NOT a true cranberry — it is a Viburnum; do not confuse the name with a Vaccinium
The European guelder-rose (Viburnum opulus) fruit is very bitter and can cause stomach upset if eaten raw or in quantity
The native American form (var. americanum, formerly V. trilobum) is the pleasant tart edible one — the two are hard to tell apart, so taste-test cautiously
Always COOK the fruit (jelly or sauce); never eat raw berries in bulk, and don't eat the seed
plants.body:
## Harvest
Find these shrubs in damp thickets, woodland edges, and hedgerows; many ornamental plantings are the European guelder-rose. Wait until after the first frosts, when the translucent red drupes have hung in their flat clusters and softened. Pick whole clusters. Taste one raw, warily: acceptable-tart means the edible American form, mouth-puckering bitterness means the European type — cook only, and sparingly.

## Prep
Always cook. Simmer the fruit, then press through a sieve to remove the single flat seed and skins. High pectin makes it set into a tart, ruby jelly that pairs with meat like real cranberry sauce. Expect a musky, sweaty odour while it cooks — it fades, and the finished jelly tastes bright.

## Notes
One flat seed per berry marks a Viburnum, not a true cranberry. The maple-shaped opposite leaves and flat flower heads are your year-round ID.

plants.title: Black Walnut
idCues: Large tree with deeply furrowed dark bark and long pinnately compound leaves (15–23 leaflets)
Nuts fall as round, tennis-ball-sized green husks — solid, not sticky-hairy
Crush a leaf or scratch a twig: aromatic, spicy-citrusy walnut smell
Husks bruise brown-black and stain everything they touch
safety: Husks contain juglone and tannins that stain skin and clothing a deep brown that won't wash out — wear gloves and old clothes.
The nut meat itself is safe and excellent; the staining/irritant issue is entirely in the husk.
Juglone is toxic to many plants and to horses' bedding — don't compost husks near a garden.
plants.body: ## Harvest Collect the round green husks off the ground once they start dropping in mid-September. Take only firm ones; skip any that are mush. Wear rubber gloves — the husks stain hands brown for a week and ruin clothing permanently. ## Prep Remove the husk first: stomp them, or roll underfoot on pavement, then peel the blackening flesh away. Wash the hard shells, then cure the nuts by drying in a single layer in a ventilated spot for 2–4 weeks. Cracking is genuinely hard work — a vise or a heavy hammer on concrete beats a normal nutcracker. The meat is rich, dark, and intensely flavored, worth the effort. ## Notes Squirrels are fast competitors, so gather early. A stained-hands session is a rite of passage. Don't dump the husks in a veggie bed — juglone suppresses many plants.

plants.title: Butternut
idCues: Close cousin of black walnut, but husks are oblong/egg-shaped, not round
Husk surface is sticky and covered in fine sticky hairs (glandular)
Lighter grey, smoother bark than black walnut; pinnately compound leaves
Nut shell is ridged and pointed at one end
safety: Same juglone/tannin staining as black walnut — the sticky husk stains skin and clothes; wear gloves.
The nut meat is safe and sweeter/oilier than black walnut.
Butternut is a declining species (butternut canker fungus) — harvest lightly and leave plenty; don't strip a healthy tree.
plants.body:
## Harvest
Gather the oblong, sticky-hairy husks from the ground in fall. The stickiness rubs off dark onto your hands, so glove up. Take a modest share only — butternut is being wiped out across its range by a canker fungus, and every surviving tree matters.

## Prep
Husk and wash as you would black walnut, then cure the shells 2–4 weeks in a dry, airy spot. The shell is hard and ridged; crack with a hammer. The meat is oilier and sweeter than black walnut — closer to a mild, buttery pecan, which is where the name comes from.

## Notes
If you find a healthy, productive butternut, note it and protect it — they're increasingly rare. Leave seed nuts behind to regenerate. Because of the oil content the meat goes rancid faster than other nuts; use or freeze it promptly.

plants.title: Shagbark Hickory
idCues: Unmistakable shaggy bark that peels away in long, curling vertical plates
Compound leaves with usually 5 leaflets (the top three larger)
Nut in a thick woody husk that splits cleanly into 4 sections when ripe
Nutshell rounded, off-white; kernel sweet like a mild pecan
safety: Don't confuse with bitternut hickory (Carya cordiformis): bitternut has smooth (not shaggy) bark and a bitter, unpalatable kernel — not toxic, just inedible and a waste of effort.
Shagbark nuts are safe and excellent raw or roasted.
Sort as you crack: discard any kernel that tastes bitter or looks discoloured/wormy.
plants.body: ## Harvest Look up for the shaggy bark, then look down — collect fallen nuts once the husks have split. Ripe husks open into four segments and release the nut cleanly. Beat the squirrels; good nuts vanish fast in a productive year. ## Prep Peel off any remaining husk, wash, and dry the nuts a week or two. Crack with a hammer or heavy nutcracker and pick the sweet kernel from the shell. It's one of the best wild nuts here — rich, sweet, pecan-like. Shell fragments are sharp, so sort carefully. ## Notes The inner bark makes a distinctive hickory-bark syrup: gently toast (don't scorch) clean bark, simmer to a tea, strain, then reduce with sugar into a smoky syrup — no tapping required. Always confirm shaggy bark; bitternut looks similar from a distance but the nut is inedibly bitter.

plants.title: Oak (Acorns)
idCues: Lobed leaves; red-oak group has bristle-tipped lobes, white-oak group has rounded lobes
Acorns sit in a scaly cap; collect only mature brown nuts, not green
White-oak-group acorns are less bitter (lower tannin) than red-oak-group
Reject any acorn with a small exit hole — that's a weevil
safety: Never eat acorns raw or unleached — they're loaded with tannins, astringent and hard on the stomach/kidneys.
Leach out tannins with repeated cold- or hot-water changes until the water runs clear and the acorn no longer tastes bitter — then they're safe.
Red-oak-group acorns need much more leaching than white-oak; both are safe once fully leached.
plants.body: ## Harvest Gather mature brown acorns off the ground in fall. Float-test at home: drop them in water and discard floaters (bug-damaged or dried out). Shell the sinkers — a slit and a squeeze pops most caps and shells off. ## Prep Leaching is mandatory. Cold leach: grind the nutmeats coarse, soak in cold water, change the water daily until it stays clear and a taste is no longer bitter (days for white oak, up to a week-plus for red oak). Hot leach is faster — boil in changes of water — but sets the starch so you can't make crisp flour after. Dry the leached meal and grind into acorn flour for breads and pancakes. ## Notes White-oak-group acorns are the beginner's choice — sweeter, faster to leach. Don't shortcut the leaching; unleached acorns taste terrible and upset the gut.

plants.title: Hazelnut
idCues: Multi-stemmed shrub with round, doubly-toothed leaves that come to a point
Nuts held in clusters wrapped in a leafy, frilled green husk (involucre)
Husks and young stems have fine bristly hairs
Nut inside is the familiar round hazelnut/filbert
safety: No toxicity concerns — hazelnuts are a common food nut.
Standard tree-nut allergen; sample cautiously if you have nut allergies.
Turkish hazel (Corylus colurna), a common Montréal street tree, also produces edible nuts in a spikier husk — safe, just fiddlier to extract.
plants.body: ## Harvest Watch the clusters from mid-August. Squirrels strip these plants clean the moment nuts approach ripeness, so pick slightly early — when the husks are still greenish but the nut inside has filled and firmed — then finish curing at home. Snap whole clusters off; the frilly husks are easy to spot. ## Prep Peel the leafy husks away (gloves help with the bristles) and spread the nuts to cure a couple of weeks until the shells harden and the kernels rattle slightly. Crack and eat raw, or roast for deeper flavor. Small but genuinely good — real hazelnuts. ## Notes Don't wait for "perfect" ripeness in the wild; you'll lose the crop to wildlife. The Turkish hazels planted along many Montréal streets are also worth checking in late summer.

plants.title: American Beech
idCues: Smooth, grey "elephant-skin" bark; often holds tan dead leaves through winter
Small triangular nuts, two per soft-spiny four-part husk
Leaves oval, glossy, with straight parallel veins ending in fine teeth
Crops vary wildly year to year — big "mast" years then near-nothing
safety: Raw beechnuts contain saponins and fagin — eating more than a small handful raw can cause stomach upset; roast them if eating a quantity.
The thin skin over the kernel is bitter and tannic — rub it off.
Safe and pleasant in small amounts raw; roasting neutralizes the irritants and improves flavor.
plants.body: ## Harvest Beech only crops heavily in periodic mast years, so some autumns there's a feast and others almost nothing. When husks litter the ground and split open, gather them — the little triangular nuts hide two to a husk. Skip flat, empty husks; a lot of nuts don't fill. ## Prep Open the soft-spiny husks and shell the nuts — fiddly work for the small reward. Rub off the bitter skin. Eat raw only a small handful at a time; to eat more, roast them, which drives off the fagin/saponins and brings out a sweet, mild flavor. Roasted beechnuts are also a classic coffee substitute when ground. ## Notes Patience is the whole game here: fill quality is low and shelling is tedious, but a good mast year is worth grabbing.

plants.title: Ginkgo
idCues: Unmistakable fan-shaped, notched leaves that turn brilliant gold in fall
Only female trees drop the fleshy, apricot-like seeds — many street trees are male and never fruit
Fallen seed pulp smells strongly of rancid butter/vomit (butyric acid)
Inside the foul pulp is a hard tan shell around a green edible kernel
safety: The fleshy seed coat causes urushiol-like contact dermatitis (same chemical family as poison ivy) — always handle with gloves, remove the flesh, and wash hands and tools.
Kernels are edible only cooked and only in small quantity: they contain ginkgotoxin (MPN), which can cause poisoning and seizures in excess.
Never eat raw. Keep adult portions small (a handful, well cooked); do not give to children — they are far more susceptible to ginkgotoxin poisoning.
plants.body: ## Harvest Only female trees drop seeds, and the smell announces them — a pungent, rancid-butter reek underfoot in October. Wear gloves before touching anything: the pulp blisters skin like poison ivy. Collect the fleshy seeds into a bag. ## Prep Gloved, squeeze or scrub the stinking flesh off under running water (outdoors — it reeks), leaving the smooth tan inner shell. Dry the shells, then crack to free the green kernel. Always cook — roast, boil, or steam — never eat raw. Wash hands, tools, and any surface the pulp touched. ## Notes Strict quantity limits: the kernels contain ginkgotoxin, so keep to a small handful even cooked, and never serve to children. Treated with respect, cooked ginkgo nuts (ginnan) are a prized delicacy — chewy, faintly bitter, jade-green. This is an advanced forage; the dermatitis and the toxin are both real.

plants.title: Common Milkweed
idCues: Stout, thick, unbranched stem when young — does not fork
Broad opposite leaves with a pale midrib, felty underside
Milky white sap oozes from any broken part
Pink-to-purple flower umbels; later warty, teardrop seed pods
Colonizes fields, roadsides and disturbed ground
safety: Eat ONLY common milkweed (A. syriaca), and only the young parts — spring shoots, unopened flower buds, and young firm pods — always COOKED, never raw.

LOOKALIKE: young dogbane (Apocynum) is toxic. Dogbane has thinner, reddish, forking/branched stems and stays slender; milkweed is stout and unbranched early. Both bleed milky sap, so sap is NOT a distinguishing test.
When in doubt on young shoots, wait for the unmistakable flower buds or pods before harvesting.
Do not eat mature pods (they turn fibrous and filled with silk) or any part raw.
plants.body:
## Harvest
Take young shoots under about 20 cm, tight unopened flower-bud clusters, and young pods that are still firm and under ~4 cm (they should squeak and have no silk inside). Snap cleanly; the plant regrows. Confirm the stout, unbranched stem and opposite leaves — never harvest a thin, forking, reddish stem, which may be toxic dogbane.

## Prep
Always cook. Boil in a change or two of water until tender; this softens texture and mellows any bitterness. Buds cook like tiny broccoli, young pods like okra, shoots like asparagus. Drain and finish in butter, soups, or stir-fries.

## Notes
Milkweed is the host plant of the monarch butterfly, so harvest lightly and leave plenty of flowering stems standing. It spreads by rhizome in large patches, so a few shoots taken from a big colony is negligible. The reward for the caution is one of the best cooked wild vegetables of the season.

plants.title: Red Clover
idCues: Rounded pink-to-magenta flower heads, egg-shaped
Trifoliate leaves (three leaflets), often with a pale V/chevron marking
Softly hairy stems and leaves
Grows in lawns, meadows, roadsides and field edges
safety: Widespread and safe; eat in moderation.
Use fresh, dry flower heads or cook young leaves — large quantities of old, damp or fermented flowers can taste off.
Contains phytoestrogens, so those who are pregnant, nursing, or on hormone-sensitive medication may prefer to keep intake light.
plants.body:
## Harvest
Pick flower heads at their peak — plump, bright magenta, and not yet browning at the base. Pinch the head off just below the bloom. Young leaves can be gathered any time in the growing season; look for the tell-tale pale chevron on the leaflets.

## Prep
Nibble fresh flowers straight off the stem for a mild sweet-pea note, or scatter them over salads. To dry for tea, spread heads on a screen out of direct sun until crisp, then store airtight; steep for a mild, hay-sweet infusion. Young leaves are best cooked briefly, like a mild green, since raw they can be tough.

## Notes
Red clover is one of the most forgiving beginner plants in Montréal — no dangerous lookalikes, and it grows in nearly every untreated lawn and meadow. Avoid patches near roadsides or sprayed turf. Bees love the blooms, so leave plenty behind.

plants.title: Wild Carrot
idCues: HAIRY stem — 'Queen Anne has hairy legs' — is the single most important tell
Whole plant, and especially the crushed root, smells distinctly of carrot
Flat-topped white umbel, often with one dark reddish/purple floret in the very center
Umbel curls up into a 'bird's nest' as it goes to seed
Three-times-divided, ferny, finely cut leaves
safety: DEADLY LOOKALIKES — this plant is in a family with two potentially FATAL relatives: poison hemlock (Conium maculatum) and water hemlock (Cicuta). Ingesting either can kill. Do not attempt this plant unless you are experienced and 100% certain.

Key tell: wild carrot has a HAIRY stem and smells like carrot. Poison hemlock has a HAIRLESS (smooth) stem with PURPLE blotches and a musty, mousy smell. Water hemlock grows in wet ground and has a chambered rootstock.
Look for the single dark reddish floret in the umbel center and the ferny carrot scent — but treat NO single feature as proof on its own; every trait must line up.
When there is any doubt at all, DO NOT harvest or eat it. The edible part is the first-year root; the dried seed can also be used as a spice.
plants.body:
## Harvest
Only for experienced foragers. The edible part is the pale first-year taproot, dug in fall from rosettes that have not yet sent up a flower stalk. Before digging, positively identify the patch the previous summer by its flowering plants: hairy stems, carrot smell, and the dark central floret. Crush a leaf and the root — it must smell unmistakably of carrot.

## Prep
First-year roots are thin, tough and woody compared to garden carrots; scrub and simmer them in soups or stocks rather than eating raw. The dried ripe seeds work as a caraway-like spice in small amounts.

## Notes
This is the most dangerous plant in this guide. Poison and water hemlock grow in the same habitats and have killed foragers who mistook them for wild carrot or wild parsnip. If you cannot confidently distinguish a hairy carrot-scented stem from a smooth purple-blotched one, leave the entire family alone.

plants.title: Garlic Mustard
idCues: Crushed leaves smell distinctly of garlic — the definitive test
First-year: low rosette of kidney-shaped, scalloped-edged leaves
Second-year: toothed, triangular leaves up a stalk topped with small white 4-petal flowers
White taproot with a faint S-shaped crook near the top
Common in shaded woodland edges, trails and gardens
safety: Invasive in Québec — forage freely and pull whole plants to help control it; bag and bin, do not compost seeding plants.
Contains mild goitrogens and trace cyanogenic compounds, so avoid eating large quantities of raw leaves daily; cooking reduces these.
Positively confirm the garlic smell — a few unrelated plants share the leaf shape but will not smell of garlic when crushed.
plants.body:
## Harvest
Pick young first-year rosette leaves and the tender tops of second-year plants in spring; both should smell of garlic when crushed. Later in the season leaves grow more bitter, so harvest early. Since it is invasive, pull the whole plant, root and all — every plant removed is a small win for the forest floor.

## Prep
Leaves go into pesto (they blend the bitterness beautifully), salads, or wilted as a green; expect a mild garlic-mustard bite. The slender white taproot, scrubbed and grated, makes a horseradish-like condiment. Cooking or blanching softens both the bitterness and the trace compounds.

## Notes
This is a guilt-free harvest: garlic mustard crowds out native spring ephemerals, so taking as much as you like is genuinely helpful. Just keep raw daily portions modest, and never re-plant or compost seeding stalks.

plants.title: Stinging Nettle
idCues: Opposite, toothed, heart-to-lance-shaped leaves with a pointed tip
Square stem and leaves covered in fine stinging hairs
Small greenish flower tassels dangle from leaf axils on older plants
Grows in moist, rich soil along streams, hedges and disturbed ground
safety: Stings on contact — wear gloves (and long sleeves) to harvest; the fine hairs inject an irritant that raises a burning welt.
Cooking or thorough drying completely destroys the sting, making the plant fully safe to eat.
Harvest tender spring tops BEFORE flowering; older/flowering nettle develops gritty mineral cystoliths that can irritate the urinary tract — avoid it.
Wood nettle (Laportea canadensis) is a similar edible with alternate leaves, but confirm your plant before eating any lookalike.
plants.body:
## Harvest
Wear gloves. Pinch or snip the top few pairs of leaves from young, non-flowering plants in spring — the tender growing tips are the prize. Collect into a bag rather than handling loose. Once plants begin to flower, stop; the texture turns gritty and the leaves are best left.

## Prep
Heat or drying kills the sting instantly. Blanch for 30–60 seconds, then use like spinach in soups, pasta, frittata, or a bright green purée; the flavour is deep and mineral. Dry the leaves for a nourishing tea. Never eat mature nettle raw.

## Notes
Stinging nettle is among the finest wild cooked greens Montréal offers, thriving in the moist rich soil along the city's ravines and riverbanks. Harvesting the tops actually encourages tender regrowth, so a well-tended patch can be picked repeatedly through spring.

plants.title: Burdock
plants.season: Fall (first-year root); early spring of year two
idCues: Huge rhubarb-like basal leaves, dull green above and woolly white-felted beneath
First-year plant is a low rosette with no flower stalk
Second-year plant sends up a tall branched stem tipped with the unmistakable hooked burrs
Crushed root and leaf smell distinctly of burdock (gobo)
safety: Don't confuse a first-year rosette with foxglove (Digitalis, toxic): burdock leaves are dull, deeply veined, woolly-white beneath and smell of burdock; foxglove leaves are toothed and lack that felt and scent
When unsure, wait for the burrs — they are unmistakable and confirm the plant
Dig only where soil is clean and untreated; roots concentrate what's in the ground
plants.body:
## Harvest
The prize is the **first-year taproot** — this is the *gobo* of Japanese cooking. Find a leafy rosette with no flower stalk and dig deep in the fall of its first year, or in the spring of year two before it bolts; once the burr stalk shoots up the root turns woody. It's a long, stubborn root, so bring a spade and lever from the side. Young leaf stalks (petioles) are edible too — cut before the plant flowers.

## Prep
Scrub the root, then peel off the bitter skin; the pale core discolours fast, so drop it in acidulated water. Slice or shave and braise, stir-fry, or add to soups — earthy and sweet. Peel leaf stalks of their stringy skin and simmer like a mild vegetable.

## Notes
Burdock is a biennial: a rosette the first year, burrs the second. The felted white leaf underside plus the burdock smell separate it from toxic foxglove. Common on disturbed ground, alleys, and vacant lots across Montréal.

plants.title: Yarrow
idCues: Soft, finely-divided feathery leaves — the 'millefeuille' (thousand-leaf) look, running all along the stem
Flat-topped clusters of small white (sometimes pale pink) flowers
Strong, distinct aromatic scent when leaves are crushed
safety: Its lacy leaves and white flat-topped flower clusters can superficially resemble toxic carrot-family plants such as poison hemlock — but yarrow's leaves are soft and feathery all along the stem and smell distinctly aromatic; confirm by the feathery leaf plus scent before use
A bitter, potent herb — use sparingly as a seasoning, tea, or medicinal
Avoid in pregnancy; can cause skin sensitivity in some people
plants.body:
## Harvest
Snip leafy tops and flower clusters through summer, ideally in the morning once the dew has dried. Take a little from many plants rather than stripping one. Yarrow grows in sunny lawns, road edges, and rough grassland all over the city.

## Prep
Think of yarrow as a bitter aromatic — a pinch goes a long way. Steep fresh or dried leaves and flowers for a grassy, slightly medicinal tea, or use finely chopped to season sparingly. Dry bunches upside down in a shaded, airy spot for winter.

## Notes
The feathery, many-divided leaf running the length of the stem, plus the strong aroma, are your safety check: poison hemlock and other toxic umbellifers have broader, glossy, non-aromatic foliage and smooth purple-blotched stems. If a plant is odourless or smells musty, walk away. Use in moderation and avoid during pregnancy.

plants.title: Pineappleweed
idCues: Low weed of paths, driveways, sidewalk cracks, and compacted soil
Cone-shaped yellow-green flower heads with NO white petals
Feathery, finely-divided leaves
Crush a flower head — it smells sweetly of pineapple and chamomile
safety: Safe and highly distinctive — the petal-less green cone plus sweet pineapple scent are unmistakable
Harvest away from roadsides, sprayed edges, and heavily trafficked paths where it often grows
plants.body:
## Harvest
Look down: pineappleweed thrives in the poorest, most trodden ground — driveways, gravel lots, and the cracks between paving stones. Pinch off the little green cone-shaped flower heads between finger and thumb through summer. Confirm every batch by crushing a head and smelling that sweet pineapple-chamomile scent.

## Prep
The flower heads make a gentle, apple-sweet tea — steep a small handful fresh, or dry them for later. They're also pleasant to nibble raw, and can be scattered over fruit or infused into syrups and shortbread. The feathery leaves are aromatic but the heads carry the best flavour.

## Notes
A close chamomile relative, but with no white ray petals — just the raised green-yellow cone. Because it favours compacted, disturbed ground right where people and cars pass, choose clean patches and give them a rinse. Abundant and easy for a first forage.

plants.title: Mugwort
idCues: Tall roadside and wasteland weed, often chest-high
Deeply lobed leaves: green above, silvery-white and woolly beneath
Grooved, often reddish stems
Sage-like aroma when leaves are crushed
safety: Contains thujone — use only in small culinary amounts
AVOID in pregnancy
A common pollen allergen; those sensitive to ragweed/Asteraceae may react
Harvest away from roadside verges where it often grows and accumulates traffic pollution
plants.body:
## Harvest
Mugwort lines railway edges, alleys, and vacant lots across Montréal, often growing waist- to chest-high by late summer. Pick young leafy tops before the plant flowers, when the flavour is cleanest. Flip a leaf to confirm the silvery-white woolly underside against the green top — the plant's signature.

## Prep
A bitter aromatic — treat it like a strong herb, not a green. A few chopped leaves season fatty meats, poultry, and rich stews (its traditional role), cutting the grease. It also makes a bitter tea. Dry sprigs for winter; the flavour concentrates, so use even less.

## Notes
Because mugwort contains thujone, keep it to small culinary quantities and avoid it entirely during pregnancy. Its late-summer pollen is a well-known allergen, so sensitive foragers should handle flowering plants with care. Silvery leaf underside plus sage-like scent make it easy to recognise once you know it.

plants.title: Wild Chives
idCues: Hollow, round, grass-like leaves growing in clumps
Pink-purple pompom flower heads
Every part smells strongly of onion when crushed
safety: ALWAYS confirm the onion/garlic smell — every part of an edible wild Allium smells strongly of onion when crushed
If there is NO onion smell, it is NOT chives and could be a toxic lookalike such as death camas or star-of-Bethlehem — do not eat
Death camas can grow among grasses and has flat (not hollow, round) leaves and no onion odour; when in doubt, discard
plants.body:
## Harvest
Wild chives grow in grassy clumps in lawns, park edges, and rocky spots, sending up hollow round leaves and, from late spring, pink-purple pompom flowers. Snip leaves with scissors a couple of centimetres above the base so the clump regrows, and pick a few flower heads. **Crush a leaf and smell it every single time** — a strong onion scent is your go/no-go test.

## Prep
Use exactly like garden chives: snip the hollow leaves raw over eggs, potatoes, salads, and soups for a mild onion bite. The purple flowers pull apart into florets that garnish and flavour dishes, and steep into a pink onion vinegar.

## Notes
The onion smell is the whole safety story. Toxic lookalikes like death camas and star-of-Bethlehem can share a grassy look but have flat leaves and no onion odour. No smell, no harvest — no exceptions.
